An authorized person of a national critical information infrastructure entity must submit the particulars of information within six hours from the time the cyber security incident comes to the knowledge of the entity [1].

* The required particulars include the authorized person's details, the entity's details (including sector and sector lead), and information on the incident such as type, description, severity, known date and time of occurrence, and method of discovery [1].

An NCII entity must conduct a cyber security risk assessment at least once a year and an audit at least once in every two years [1].

* Risk assessments must be conducted at least once a year [1].
* Audits must be carried out at least once in every two years, or at a higher frequency if directed by the Chief Executive in any particular case [1].

Information must be submitted through the National Cyber Coordination and Command Centre System [1].

* If there is a disruption in the National Cyber Coordination and Command Centre System, submission shall be made by the communication as determined by the Chief Executive [1].

A person who provides a cyber security service without a licence commits an offence and is liable to a fine not exceeding five hundred thousand ringgit or imprisonment for a term not exceeding ten years or both [1].

* This penalty also applies to anyone who advertises or holds himself out as a provider of a cyber security service without a licence [1].

A licensee must retain records for a period of not less than six years from the date the cyber security service was provided [1].

* Records must be kept and maintained in the manner determined by the Chief Executive [1].
* Records must be produced to the Chief Executive at any time as directed [1].

Yes, the Act has effect outside as well as within Malaysia regardless of the person's nationality or citizenship [1].

* A person who commits an offence under this Act outside Malaysia may be dealt with as if the offence was committed within Malaysia [1].
* This application occurs if the national critical information infrastructure involved in the offence is wholly or partly in Malaysia [1].

A cyber security incident is defined as an act or activity carried out on or through a computer or computer system, without lawful authority, that jeopardizes or adversely affects the cyber security of that computer or computer system or another computer or computer system [1].

An NCII entity must notify its national critical information infrastructure sector lead of a material change within thirty days from the date the change was completed [1].

* A change is considered material if it affects or may affect the cyber security of the NCII or the entity's ability to respond to a cyber security threat or incident [1].

An NCII entity that fails to comply with the Chief Executive's directions during a cyber security exercise commits an offence and is liable to a fine not exceeding one hundred thousand ringgit [1].

* The Chief Executive may give directions to the NCII entity as he thinks fit for the purpose of the cyber security exercise [1].
* Failure to comply with these directions results in a fine not exceeding one hundred thousand ringgit upon conviction [1].

You must notify the Chief Executive and your national critical information infrastructure sector lead of the incident [1].

* Immediately, by electronic means, give a notification of the cyber security incident when it comes to the knowledge of the entity [2].
* Within six hours from the time the incident comes to the knowledge of the entity, submit particulars including the authorized person, the entity, sector, sector lead, and information on the incident (type, description, severity, known date/time of occurrence, and method of discovery) [2].
* Within fourteen days after the initial notification, provide supplementary information to the fullest extent practicable, including affected NCII particulars, estimated number of hosts affected, threat actor particulars, artifacts, related incidents, tactics, techniques and procedures, impact, and action taken [2].
* Provide further updates on the incident from time to time as the Chief Executive may require [2].

Yes, a person responsible for the management of a body of persons may be charged severally or jointly with that body for an offence under the Act [1].

* A national critical information infrastructure entity commits an offence if it fails to comply with a directive from the Chief Executive regarding measures to respond to, recover from, or prevent a cyber security incident [2].
* If the entity is a company, limited liability partnership, firm, society or other body of persons, a director, manager, or other similar officer responsible for management may be charged [1].
* Such a person shall be deemed guilty and liable to the same punishment as an individual unless they prove the offence was committed without their knowledge, or without their consent or connivance and that they exercised due diligence to prevent it [1].
* The penalty for failing to comply with the Chief Executive's directive is a fine not exceeding two hundred thousand ringgit, imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both [2].

A national critical information infrastructure sector lead may designate a person or Government Entity as a national critical information infrastructure entity [1].

* A designated entity must notify its sector lead in writing without delay if it believes its computer or computer system has ceased to be a national critical information infrastructure or if it no longer owns or operates any national critical information infrastructure [1].

You must immediately notify the Chief Executive and your national critical information infrastructure sector lead by electronic means [1], [2].

* Within six hours of the incident coming to your knowledge, you must submit particulars of the authorized person, the NCII entity, the NCII sector, the NCII sector lead, and information on the incident (type, description, severity, known date/time of occurrence, and method of discovery) [1].
* Within fourteen days after the initial notification, you must provide supplementary information to the fullest extent practicable, including affected NCII particulars, estimated number of affected hosts, threat actor particulars, artifacts, related incidents, tactics, techniques and procedures, impact on the NCII or computer systems, and actions taken [1].
* Information for the six-hour and fourteen-day requirements must be submitted through the National Cyber Coordination and Command Centre System, or via communication determined by the Chief Executive if that system is disrupted [3].
* You must provide further updates on the incident from time to time as required by the Chief Executive [1].

A person or Government Entity must first be designated as a national critical information infrastructure entity under section 17 or 18 [1].

* A national critical information infrastructure sector lead may designate a person as a national critical information infrastructure entity if they are satisfied that the person owns or operates a national critical information infrastructure [2].
* The Chief Executive may designate a national critical information infrastructure sector lead as a national critical information infrastructure entity if they are satisfied that the sector lead owns or operates a national critical information infrastructure [3].

Failure to comply with cyber security risk assessment and audit requirements can result in fines or imprisonment [1].

* Contravention of the duty to conduct a cyber security risk assessment and audit, or the failure to submit the resulting reports to the Chief Executive within thirty days, carries a penalty of a fine not exceeding two hundred thousand ringgit, imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both [1].
* Failure to comply with directions from the Chief Executive to re-evaluate risks, rectify an insufficient audit report, or conduct additional assessments/audits carries a penalty of a fine not exceeding one hundred thousand ringgit [1].
